title: Aesthetics
description: In this panel we examine what kinds of stories games tend to tell, how they tell those stories,and why we keep coming back, with a particular focus on violence, power dynamics,mechanical expression, and aesthetics. Join us for a procedurally-generated series of talkscovering the what, why, and how of storytelling in games, followed by an audience-directedroundtable discussion where we put you, the players, in charge.

abstracts.title: Claire Lincoln
abstracts.description:
Claire Lincoln

Video games often make players feel powerful. Players wield awesome abilities, assumethe role of competent heroes, and make meaningful choices. These expressions of power oftenconstruct a fantasy for the player to revel in and are amplified by interactivity, a staple of themedium. Prior research lays the groundwork for interactivity to be a meaningful source of power,awarding players a sense of agency over the experience. This paper operates under theunderstanding that the video game medium is primed and even expected to uphold player agencyand fantasies of power. And, to offer insight into the role of interactivity, this paper explores acollection of games that subvert these fantasies, challenge player agency and recontextualizepower as an undesirable experience.

This paper demonstrates how games like Mouthwashing and Horses challenge playeragency by deliberately restricting player choice and forcing participation in disturbing scenarios.Notably, these are violent games; however, violence is treated not as a justified application ofpower, but rather as a source of discomfort and uncomfortable truths. Silent Hill 2 accomplishesa similar feat, inviting the player into a fantasy only to recontextualize their actions in the game’sfinal moments, stripping away violence’s justification and recasting the hero as weak andculpable. Similarly, other examined titles subvert the appeal of playing a likable and competentcharacter, challenging any sense of power the player may gain through identifying with theiravatar. Agency, rather than a source of empowerment, constructs an experience that is full oftension and reflection, a total subversion of the fantasy players have come to expect.

Ultimately, this paper proposes that video games, through their unique employment ofinteractivity and promise of player agency, are especially effective at critiquing power andviolence. By disrupting traditional power fantasies, these works encourage players to reflect ontheir expectations of control, their desire for power, and the ethics of virtual violence.

abstracts.title: George Eltzroth
abstracts.description:
George Eltzroth

By now, videogames are well past their infancy. The medium is host to myriad works thatleverage its unique narrative capabilities to tell personal, resonant, and affecting stories. Despitethis, the academic field of game studies, fledgeling though it may be in the context of academia,is far more developed than the related field of game analysis. This is a work of game analysis.The intention of this paper is to name, and define two techniques for storytelling that are uniqueto videogames: emergence and embodiment, and contextualize their place in the greaterlineage of writing and analysis on games, procedurality, and storytelling. I will then examinewhen and how they are employed by playing and analyzing three illustrative games. Those casestudies are: Blaseball, Children of the Sun, and Far: Lone Sails, three games which use thesestorytelling techniques to different extents and with different levels of visibility, creating a broadportrait of how existing games tell stories.

abstracts.title: Zhili Chen
abstracts.description:
Zhili Chen

Violence has long been a central component of game design, yet it is often treated primarilyas a mechanic of challenge or spectacle rather than as a meaningful expressive tool. This project investigates violence as a form of expression in games, asking how violent systemscan convey emotion, character, and narrative rather than merely serve as interactive conflict resolution.

This research contributes to ongoing discourse by reframing violence not as content alone,but as a designed language embedded within player interaction. Drawing from analyses ofexisting games, film theory, and interactive media studies, the project examines how timing,player agency, repetition, and feedback systems shape the emotional and narrative meaningof violent acts. Particular attention is given to how systems of escalation, loss of control, andembodiment can transform violence into a vehicle for expressing psychological states.The practical component of this research is a prototype game that situates combat within theeveryday life of a troubled high school student. In this work, fighting is not the primary goalbut one aspect of a broader simulation, where player actions accumulate toward moments ofloss of control, represented through a “possession” system. This design explores how violencecan emerge from systemic pressure rather than player intention alone.

The findings suggest that when integrated with narrative systems and player state, violencecan function as a powerful expressive medium, capable of communicating internal conflictand social tension. This project demonstrates how recontextualizing violence can expand itsrole within game design beyond spectacle toward meaningful expression.

title: Industry
description: Games are much more than the software we interact with - they’re the people who make them,the corporations greenlighting them, and the financial structures that can both make thempossible and interfere with their core design in the same breath. Beginning with individualpresentations, this panel will seek to explore each of those topics through a multitude ofperspectives. Destin will talk about the explosion of live-service games in the post-pandemicdigital games industry, connecting a throughline to the eventual mass layoffs that plagued theindustry in its wake. Madeline will draw comparisons between the Hollywood film industry andthe modern gaming industry through the lens of its employees: What can we learn from moredeveloped creative industries about how best to protect the people working within it from bothinternal and external harm? Abhi will dive into “gacha” game design and how it stems from theeconomy of time, going deep into the pity system and eventually exploring ways of doing ethicalgacha design. Finally, Peyton will bring us into the world of analog gaming, giving an extensivestudy of Kickstarter through its top 100 board games to discover common trends and form apicture of what a successful campaign might look like in the modern Kickstarter environment.After individual presentations, the entire panel will come together to talk amongst themselves ina roundtable discussion that will afterwards be open to audience involvement.

abstracts.title: Abhishek Chatterjee
abstracts.description:
Abhishek Chatterjee

The 'Free-to-Play' (F2P) mobile games industry is built on a difficult conflict: the desire todesign a fun game versus the pressure to design a profitable product. This tension is mostobvious in Gacha mechanics. Developers often pitch mechanics like the 'Pity System', whichguarantees a drop after a certain number of failed pulls, as a safety net for players. However,critics usually dismiss these systems as predatory gambling. This back-and-forth ignores thecomplex reasons players actually choose to engage with these games and the specific UI tricksused to keep them spending.

This paper bridges the disconnect between industry PR and academic critics by combining mypersonal experience as a former mobile systems designer with academic research. Using afractal approach, the paper first looks at Gacha through the broader 'Economy of Time,'exploring how modern players rationalize spending money just to skip the grind. It thenexamines the core F2P ecosystem, showing how early-game 'fun' pivots into aggressivemonetization once a player becomes a veteran. Finally, it breaks down the specific UI of the PitySystem, showing how it hides real-world costs and weaponizes the player's sunk time.

By applying an ethical framework to these systems, the paper concludes that 'Ethical Gacha' ispossible. It proposes a set of 'Ethical Design Pillars', focusing on absolute transparency andhard financial caps, arguing that sustainable design must respect the player's agency ratherthan relying on deceptive mechanics.

abstracts.title: Destin Piagentini
abstracts.description:
Destin Piagentini

Leading up to the Covid-19 pandemic, the digital gaming industry had enjoyed a period ofcontinued growth in both player acquisition and resource investment. That upward trajectory notonly continued through the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic, but surged as a result of it.While players were stuck at home, it became easier to devote their time to entertainment that wasaccessible from their living rooms. At the same time, corporate relief efforts made expansion lessrisky for the companies steering the industry to pump more resources to meet the expandeddemand as a result of the increased time commitment from its players. Eager to spend funds,industry leaders began to set their sights on live-service games as an emerging trend. Inopposition to the traditional model of digital games as finite experiences, live-service-gamesseek to deliver multiplayer experiences that are meant to be played repeatedly as they evolvethrough seasonal up-dates that add new gameplay variations of the core experience. For gamepublishers, a successful live-service game with ongoing revenue opportunities is an attractiveachievement to pursue, but, because these games rely on massive playerbases to support them(often in lieu of an upfront fee), achieving success in this genre has become increasingly difficultas the most popular games are focused on monopolizing the time of their players. As a result,major publishers such as PlayStation Studios have tried to ensure a “hit” through sheer quantity,betting that an investment made in many life-service projects will yield at least one game thatcan generate the profits they’re seeking. In reality, the high difficulty in achieving success forthese games mean that most projects are either cancelled before or shortly after they are releasedto the public. The resulting pivot in strategy leaves the developers of those projects often withoutjobs or stressed to quickly find a new lucrative project on short-notice.

In my new-games journalism piece, I will directly connect the Covid-19 pandemic to therapid expansion and ensuing deflation of the digital gaming industry through the renewed focuson investments into live-service gaming, giving context by analyzing the emergence of thelive-service trend and examining how the pandemic’s early days served as both a powerful andunsustainable boon to the industry but extracted a heavier toll as the macroeconomicenvironment soured for both consumers and companies. Concluding my findings, I will offer ahumanistic perspective on how these broader trends affect the developers working in thisindustry who are, by and large, caught in the crossfire of rapidly changing corporate mandatesand are often left to suffer the largest consequences of their failure.

In my conference presentation, I will briefly summarize these findings before discussingthem amongst other industry challenges in a panel with my peers.

abstracts.title: Madeline Khare
abstracts.description:
Madeline Khare

Flashing lights, limousines, and iconic outfits: celebrities of the early 2000s seemingly had it all. That is, until the paparazzi told us otherwise. Paparazzi feasted off of disproving the so-called perfect lives of primarily women celebrities, to the point they would do anything to get potentially damaging photos to sell to tabloids. These women were stalked, doxed, even live-streamed at their own homes without permission - all so jealous hate-mongerers could critique them to feel better about themselves. Then, less than a decade later in 2014, Gamergate begins. Gamergate is a misogynistic online harassment campaign attacking several women or nonbinary people who were considered successful in their respective games careers. Anonymous “trolls” on forums like 4chan doxed the targets of Gamergate, allowing others to send violent threats directly to their residences. Fast forward another decade, in the 2020’s, there has been a clear shift in the way paparazzi are regarded among Hollywood professionals and the public eye - where it was once revered to photograph a young celebrity’s underwear as she got out of a limousine, now that is an offense punishable by law in several states. Meanwhile, in the games industry where fewer legal action has been taken, experts predict a second Gamergate is coming. This essay will seek to examine what legal gains Hollywood took in order to protect women from harassment in the workplace, and determine if such legal actions could prove useful in the games industry.

abstracts.title: Peyton Schwiebert
abstracts.description:
Peyton Schwiebert

What are the commonalities between the most successful tabletop kickstarters of alltime? What does a modern kickstarter look like in comparison to the original concept of theplatform? What attracts people to crowdfunding games? To answer these questions, researchtook the form of a spreadsheet compiling together data about the top board games on thecrowdfunding website, kickstart, and subsequent data about the game from the website boardgame geek, a compiler of player opinion and wiki resource for all things tabletop. By compilinginformation about the top 100 most successful tabletop games on kickstarter, commonalities ingenre, theme, timing, and attachment to other intellectual properties, along with other factors,can be found. This trend towards prebuilt fanbases in particular shows a change in kickstarterfrom a indie game crowdfunding platform into almost a new form of preorder website, allowinglarger companies to use FOMO on limited time objects to gain more money from the consumer.This can be seen in comparison who has run these kickstarters, and contrasting the price of a“base” game to the average amount donated by backers in order to get limited time add ons.Finally, the research is concluded through an averaging of all of the common attributes in orderto create the next (potential) top 100 kickstarter campaign.

title: Identity
description:
Our panel will be discussing how certain concepts are represented in gamesand why they’re represented that way. Each panelist will be covering adifferent aspect of the self and examining how players explore said aspectsin and outside of games.

To start, we will have the audience play a version of HARVL, a socialdeduction game with roleplaying elements. This will contextualize ouridentity-focused presentations.

Esteban will use the affordances of role-playing games to understand whyFacebook’s version of the Metaverse was largely unsuccessful. Though manyRPGs – from tabletop to MMOs – already provide a safe and shared space forpersonal expression, what is the role of technology in creating 'limitless”social worlds?

Mars will examine the Bioshock series to analyze how the heroic fatherprotagonist and the systematic erasure/demonization of motherhood doesnot necessarily celebrate fatherhood — rather, “exceptional” male parenting issimply ordinary maternal expectations rebranded as “heroism”.

Lucas will draw on the principles of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy as a lens toexplore how mental illness can be taught and represented in games withoutthe stigma and horror tied to it. He will develop a framework and apply it toexamine how Depression Quest portrays the struggles of depression notthrough psychological horror imagery, but through its procedural rhetoric.

Despoina/DLC will discuss representation of gender in nonhuman characters and analyze how it leads to gender and identity play in Pokémonfans both in-game and IRL. She will examine cosplay, in particular Pokémoncosplay drag (PokeDrag), as a way in which queer Pokemon fans co-opt and co-createthe identities of these creatures alongside the designers.

We will conclude with a brief Q&A session with all panelists. The audiencewill be asked to allow their HARVL roles to guide how they behave duringthe Q&A!

abstracts.title: Despoina/DLC
abstracts.description:
Pokémon, first released during 1996 in versions Red, Green, and later Blue, isa well-beloved video game and transmedia franchise that has amassed allkinds of fans over its 30-year-and-counting lifetime. This presentation aims to discuss the evolution of gender and identity play among Pokémonfans. To that end, I examine five major design choices that have been madeto dictate how gender is represented in the Pokémon world. These are:

● 1996-Now: The introduction and function of Pokémon gender as amechanic

● 2000/2001: The ability to choose the gender of your player character

● 2013: The ability to customize your character avatar

● 2016-2019: The introduction of the first non-binary Pokémon trainer inPokémon GO

● 2025: The advent of gender-neutral clothing in Pokémon Legends: ZA,Pokémon’s latest main series title

My investigation of these features leads me to observe one way Pokémonfans transition their in-game gender and identity play to the physical world. Irefer to the growing Pokémon cosplay drag (or simply, PokéDrag) scene,found in New York City and other cities with vibrant drag communities.Research done to support this analysis includes interviews with queerPokémon fans, as well as academic writing on cosplay/drag, Pokémon andgender representation in games, and the role of Pokémon fan works. This isall in service of my argument that queer Pokémon fans deepen theirrelationship with the source material and by extension, themselves, byco-opting and co-creating the identities of these non-human characters.

My conference contribution will feature a presentation that functions as ascoped down version of the larger video essay and will conclude with aPokéDrag performance from yours truly to further contextualize my thesis.

abstracts.title: Esteban Romero
abstracts.description:
Esteban Romero

The Metaverse is a vision of a digital universe popularized in 2021 after Facebook rebranded itself and announced it as their next social platform. They claimed that people could do anything together in this digital universe – from business to education. A few years later, the company is downscaling their Reality Labsdivision and their proprietary VR social app, Horizon Worlds, has been called 'dead' by major media outlets. In this work, I will analyze the Metaverse beyond itstechnical challenges to understand its failure as a vision and a culture: a'technofuturistic dream' of a post-racial, hyper-connected, and limitless VRutopia. By comparing this ideal to the worlds of role-playing games, I support thethesis that the metaverse was largely unsuccessful because it was pitched as away for people to perform real-world activities and lacked the social structuresafforded by rules. RPGs, on the contrary, tend to provide a safe and isolated spacefor play, socialization, emergent storytelling, and identity expression. Throughour creativity and capacity for social negotiation, we can use games to transformany social experience into a shared fantasy. This leads me to conclude that a partof Meta’s original vision already exists in the context of RGPs and it can be realizedwithout the need for technology.
